claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Single-phase ZrB2 has limited oxidation resistance.
Single-phase ZrB2 has limited resistance to corrosion by liquid plating metals.
Adding approximately 2–3 wt% Si and using SPS at about 1600 °C will enhance ZrB2 densification through a transient liquid phase.
Liquid-phase-assisted mass transport can promote ceramic densification.
Si will segregate to ZrB2 grain boundaries during cooling.
The segregated Si will form a continuous, adherent SiO2-rich intergranular film after oxidation.
The SiO2-rich layer will shield the ZrB2 matrix from further high-temperature oxidation.
The SiO2-rich layer will protect ZrB2 from corrosion by liquid plating metals.
Si-doped ZrB2 sintered at about 1600 °C will attain densification comparable to ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C.
Si-doped ZrB2 sintered at about 1600 °C will retain strength and structural integrity comparable to conventionally high-temperature-sintered ZrB2.
Si-doped ZrB2 will have markedly better oxidation resistance than conventional ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
Si-doped ZrB2 will have markedly better durability in liquid plating-metal baths than conventional ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
Reducing the manufacturing temperature to about 1600 °C will improve processing economics and energy efficiency.
The proposed material can serve under oxidizing conditions up to approximately 1600 °C.
The proposed material can serve in liquid plating-metal environments.
Excess Si or poorly controlled sintering parameters may produce undesirable secondary phases.
Precisely controlling Si content and sintering parameters will avoid deleterious silicide phases.
The long-term stability of the SiO2-rich film under cyclic thermal and corrosive exposure is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The structural-mediator field suggests that a SiO2-rich film forms upon cooling, although cooling occurs under an inert/reducing atmosphere; the mechanism field instead requires a later oxidation step. The timing and environment of film formation are therefore inconsistent or insufficiently distinguished.
